Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Value Name: Mature IXP ecosystem with broad participation
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original Source urls field is malformed/truncated (pulse.internetsociety.org/...KE is not a resolvable URL). Verified independently via Packet Clearing House, PeeringDB and Internet Society Pulse IXP Tracker: KIXP (Nairobi) was established February 2001, is managed by TESPOK, and has 132-135 recorded members/peers (including Amazon, Meta, ByteDance, Huawei Cloud, MTN/Bayobab and numerous local ISPs and banks) with roughly 2.9 Tbps of peering capacity. This is consistent with 'mature IXP ecosystem with broad participation'. Score of 5 confirmed; source URLs corrected.
revised_comments: Kenya's Internet Exchange Point (KIXP), based in Nairobi and established in February 2001, is managed by the Technology Service Providers Association of Kenya (TESPOK). It is a mature exchange with over 130 peering members recorded on PeeringDB, including global content and cloud networks (Amazon, Meta, ByteDance, Huawei Cloud) alongside domestic ISPs and banks, exchanging traffic at multi-terabit capacity. This reflects a mature IXP ecosystem with broad participation.

Definition: The availability and presence of major cloud service providers (hyperscale and regional) operating in or serving the country with local or near-local infrastructure. Cloud availability determines access to scalable computing resources for government, business, and startups.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited; a single light check surfaced clearly authoritative evidence of cloud presence, so it was moved to the full verification path. AWS launched a Local Zone in Nairobi (af-south-1-nbo-1a, parent region Cape Town) in 2022, giving an operational hyperscale edge presence, plus AWS Outposts (2022). Oracle announced (Jan 2024) and is building, via host partner iXAfrica, a full OCI public cloud region in Nairobi, but as of April 2026 no live launch date has been confirmed. With one major provider confirmed live locally and a second in build-out but not yet operational, scored 4 (at least one major provider with local presence or edge node) rather than 5.
revised_comments: Kenya has an operational hyperscale cloud edge presence via an AWS Local Zone in Nairobi (launched 2022, parent region Cape Town), supplemented by AWS Outposts. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is building a full public cloud region in Nairobi in partnership with iXAfrica Data Centres, announced in 2024 and in active construction, though not yet live. Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud continue to serve Kenya from regional data centres, principally in South Africa, without a local availability zone.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited; a single light check surfaced clearly authoritative evidence, so it was moved to the full verification path. Kenya's Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019) established the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC), which has issued numerous published enforcement determinations and administrative fines against data controllers/processors (e.g. Safaricom and Becton Dickinson each fined KES 250,000, Feb 2025; cumulative fines of over KES 26 million 2022-2024; further determinations through late 2025). This is an active enforcement record on top of enacted legislation and an established authority, supporting a score of 5.
revised_comments: Kenya's Data Protection Act, 2019 gives effect to Article 31(c) and (d) of the Constitution and establishes the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) as an independent regulator. The ODPC actively enforces the Act, publishing complaint determinations and imposing administrative fines on data controllers and processors, including cumulative fines exceeding KES 26 million between 2022 and 2024 and further enforcement actions, for example against Safaricom and Becton Dickinson East Africa, through 2025. This constitutes a mature legislative and enforcement framework.

Definition: The presence and tier quality of commercial/colocation data center facilities operating in the country. Commercial data centers provide the physical infrastructure for hosting cloud services, content delivery, and enterprise applications domestically.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited; a single light check surfaced clearly authoritative evidence, so it was moved to the full verification path. Nairobi hosts multiple established commercial colocation facilities: Africa Data Centres' NBO1 (Uptime Institute Tier III certified, 4 data halls, ~7.5MW site capacity), iColo's NBO1 (280-rack, carrier-neutral, opened 2019), and iXAfrica's NBOX1 (22.5MW total capacity, hyperscale/AI-ready, described as the largest such facility in East and Central Africa). Multiple Tier III+ operators with hyperscale-scale capacity supports a score of 5 (mature data centre market with multiple operators and hyperscale presence).
revised_comments: Nairobi hosts a mature commercial data centre market with multiple established operators. Africa Data Centres operates a Tier III-certified facility (NBO1) with around 7.5MW of available capacity; iColo operates a carrier-neutral, 280-rack colocation facility in Karen (NBO1), opened in 2019; and iXAfrica operates a 22.5MW hyperscale, AI-ready campus on Mombasa Road, positioned as the region's largest such facility and selected to host Oracle's forthcoming public cloud region. This multi-operator, hyperscale-capable market supports a wide range of colocation, connectivity and cloud hosting needs.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Value Name: Very Expensive (>10% of household income for basic service)
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The two cited sources (GNI per capita and a retail electricity price) were never combined into a documented calculation supporting the 'Very Expensive (>10%)' score. Recalculating: KPLC's EPRA-approved 2025/26 residential tariffs are KES 12.23/kWh (lifeline, up to 30 units/month), KES 16.45/kWh (30-100 units) and KES 19.08/kWh (100+ units), excluding levies/VAT; GlobalPetrolPrices' blended residential price, inclusive of all taxes and levies, is around USD 0.216/kWh (December 2025). Against World Bank GNI per capita, Atlas method, of USD 2,090 (2024, ~USD 174/month), a basic consumption band of 30-50 kWh/month costs roughly 3.7-6.2% of monthly per-capita GNI — pointing to code 2 (Expensive, 5-10%) or code 3 (Moderate, 2-5%), not code 1. Because the result is sensitive to the assumed 'basic service' consumption threshold and to whether household or per-capita income is the correct denominator (household income is typically higher than per-capita income), this is flagged for human review rather than asserting a specific replacement code.
revised_comments: Kenya Power (KPLC) applies EPRA-approved tiered residential tariffs: KES 12.23/kWh for lifeline consumption up to 30 units/month, KES 16.45/kWh for 30-100 units, and KES 19.08/kWh above 100 units (all exclusive of levies and VAT), with a blended residential price inclusive of taxes and levies of around USD 0.216/kWh as of December 2025. Kenya's GNI per capita (Atlas method) was USD 2,090 in 2024, equivalent to roughly USD 174 per month.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Original score of 0/Unknown cited only a 2016 rural figure (39%) with no urban comparator, so no gap could be calculated at the time. World Bank data (WDI series EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS, via TradingEconomics/CountryDataHub) give access to electricity, urban (% of urban population) at 96.0% and rural (% of rural population) at 67.9%, both for 2023 — a gap of 28.1 percentage points, corresponding to code 3 (Gap 21-40pp). Afrobarometer's 2024 survey corroborates a substantial urban-rural divide using different measures (grid proximity and reliable supply rather than simple access): 98% vs 82% grid proximity and 90% vs 51% actual KPLC connection for urban vs rural respondents. Score revised from 0 to 3.
revised_comments: Kenya has a moderate urban-rural electrification gap. World Bank data for 2023 show 96.0% of the urban population with access to electricity compared with 67.9% of the rural population, a gap of around 28 percentage points. Afrobarometer's 2024 survey corroborates a substantial divide by other measures: 98% of urban respondents live within reach of the national grid versus 82% of rural respondents, and actual household connection rates are 90% (urban) versus 51% (rural).
